extracted.intended_audience: novelists; students of fiction; creative-writing practitioners and critics
extracted.subtask_description: Advice on choosing and managing the 'pictorial' (panoramic, narrator-present) versus the 'dramatic' (author-effacing, scene-enacted) methods in novel-writing, including handling of climax, point of view, time, and the use of incidental detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of incidental sketches vs deliberate scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: When sketching a train of life in broad free strokes, brief incidents — "a hint, a moment, a glance" — can suffice; the writer often brushes past definite recollections without particularizing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ quick, illustrative glimpses that "spring up" in memory to enrich the narrative without dwelling on them; these should illustrate and reinforce the broad effect rather than form fully dramatized episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climactic scenes must be enacted, not summarized
rubrics_metrics.description: The final scene cannot be recalled and summarized in an indirect, reminiscential manner; "it must be placed immediately before us" to have proper emphasis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve direct, present enactment for climaxes: place characters "immediately before us" and let them act their own parts rather than relying on the narrator's account to deliver the force of the answer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare characters to avoid forced theatrics
rubrics_metrics.description: If the novelist has not rendered characters in immediate terms beforehand, they will need to "make an unnatural effort" when finally brought forward, producing an artificial, theatrical look.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop characters' independence and presence throughout so that when they are required to carry a scene they can do so without crude devices or exaggerated emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreshortening/generalizing and subordination to broad effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The pictorial art relies on "foreshortening and generalizing, that fusion of detail, that subordination of the instance and the occasion to the broad effect."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When working panoramically, subordinate specific instances to the overall impression; use memory-like flashes and fused detail to create a sweeping picture rather than fully enacted particularities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow scenes to show themselves plainly for maximum impact
rubrics_metrics.description: A "straight, unhampered view" lets the scene "show itself, fairly and squarely," lending force to the disaster or consequence that follows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For pivotal social or dramatic moments, give the reader unobstructed ocular evidence rather than filtering everything through narratorly commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not waste major occasions or dramatic opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: Great occasions (e.g., the Waterloo ball) are "a wonderful gift for a novelist" and must not be dissipated or left to "constitute no effect whatever."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify events that logically crown the story and treat them as substantive contributions to plot and meaning rather than decorative interludes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use flexible chronology and shifting focus to create time-pictures
rubrics_metrics.description: Time-pictures are made by "leisurely play with the chronology of the story" and "shifting of the focus," so that time can be shown as tranquillity rather than sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To convey depth and stored-up time, roam to and fro in narrative order and vary focal distance (near/far) to create layers of time instead of strict chronology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose between pictorial (author-present) and dramatic (author-effacing) methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Picture and drama are contrasting manners: in picture the reader faces the story-teller; in drama the reader "turns towards the story and watches it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide which relation you want your reader to have (listening to an authorial presence versus watching events unfold) and shape narration, dialogue, and disclosure accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticate the narrator when using the pictorial method
rubrics_metrics.description: A pictorial book that makes the omniscient author conspicuous risks leaving the point of view "unaccountable"; the remedy is to "dramatize the seeing eye" or include the point of view within the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the narrator's knowledge is prominent, provide verifiable means (a dramatized observer, an internalized viewpoint, or narrative devices) that make the narrator's perspective a fact in the story, not an external intrusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve dramatic enactment (scenes) for important occasions
rubrics_metrics.description: "Drama is the novelist’s highest light... to use it prodigally where it is not needed is to lessen its force where it is essential."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hoard dramatic scenes; use them sparingly for climactic and genuinely intense moments rather than as routine devices throughout the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skill lies in managing transitions between picture and drama
rubrics_metrics.description: The quality of a novelist appears in "his management of the two, how he guides the story into the scene, how he picks it out of the scene," producing a richer story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice guiding the narrative into enacted scenes and resuming panoramic overview smoothly so that the back-and-forth enhances rather than disrupts coherence and intensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid both neglect and overuse of the scene
rubrics_metrics.description: In fiction "the treatment of the scene is neglected, and yet it recurs again and again, much too often, and its value is wasted."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft individual scenes with care when they occur, and avoid inserting scenes merely by habit; each scene should be necessary and well-realized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make point of view objective to prevent loose ends
rubrics_metrics.description: To silence questioning of the narrator's authority, "make the mind and the eye objective, to make them facts in the story."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate the narrator's vantage into the fiction (e.g., via an identifiable observer or verifiable perspective) so readers can recognize and verify the source of the narrative's knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a detached spectator when doing panoramic vistas
rubrics_metrics.description: A panorama of manners requires "some detached spectator, who looks on from without" to justify the wide, sweeping view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When covering large social or temporal landscapes, supply a believable vantage (narrator or character) whose observations legitimize the breadth of coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match method to intention: drama for intensity, picture for breadth
rubrics_metrics.description: "If we wish to see an abundance and multitude of life we shall find it more readily... by looking for an hour into a memory" (picture); drama is for single intense enactment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose pictorial method to convey breadth and multiplicity; choose dramatic enactment when you need immediacy and concentrated intensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessarily strained omniscience and intrusive narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: By convention the author has universal knowledge, but a "prudent novelist does not strain it unnecessarily" — excessive authorial presence can give the book an "inconclusive look" and a thin general impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit intrusive authorial flourishes; where omniscience is used, avoid drawing attention to the narrator's authority in ways that weaken the book's internal completeness, especially on rereading.
